planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Kahuna is a California-bred purple passionfruit selection valued for unusually large, high-quality fruit on a vigorous, self-fertile vine.

directions: Train Kahuna onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, giving the fast-climbing tendrils ample room to cover a large support structure. This selection was bred in California for exceptionally large, medium-purple fruit with a sweet, subacid flavor, bearing well on a single self-fertile plant without a second vine for pollination. Like other purple passionfruit types it fruits from cuttings within about a year and benefits from regular tip-pruning to channel growth onto the support rather than into a tangled mass. In zone 9 gardens, site it in the warmest, most sheltered spot and mulch heavily into winter, since purple passionfruit can be killed back hard by a freeze.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Passionfruit Production

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Nancy Garrison is a purple passionfruit noted among home growers for unusually good cold tolerance for a P. edulis selection, making it a solid candidate for Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Plant Nancy Garrison against a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, since established vines climb vigorously and can cover 10 to 20 feet in a season. It is self-fertile and sets round, egg-sized, purple-skinned fruit with tart-sweet, orange pulp continuously through the warm months once mature, without needing a second passionfruit for cross-pollination. Established plants have shown better recovery from brief cold spells than many other purple passionfruit selections, a useful trait at the edge of its range, though young vines still need frost protection their first winter or two. Keep soil evenly moist during fruit set and prune back congested growth each spring to renew fruiting wood.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants well after the last frost, once nights are reliably warm, at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence; Waimanalo is a University of Hawaii yellow passionfruit selection grown widely for juice production in frost-free, subtropical-to-tropical climates.

directions: Give Waimanalo a strong trellis or fence in full sun and warm, well-drained soil, since this yellow-fruited selection needs more consistent heat than the hardier purple passionfruit types and sulks in cool conditions. It was developed by the University of Hawaii from several high-performing strains and is grown commercially for its large, canary-yellow fruit and strongly aromatic, tart juice. Unlike many purple passionfruit selections it is only partially self-fertile, so hand-pollination or a companion vine improves fruit set, especially in home gardens without many visiting bees. Protect vines from any cold exposure, as yellow passionfruit is noticeably more cold-sensitive than purple types and is best reserved for the warmest, most frost-free corners of a zone 9b-10 Gulf Coast garden.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR Cooperative Extension Service
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden

planting.note: Plant container vines well after the last frost in warm, humid conditions and well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Sunburst is a frost-tender hybrid of Passiflora gilbertiana and P. jorullensis bred by Patrick Worley and needs winter protection anywhere temperatures approach freezing.

directions: Grow Sunburst on a trellis, arbor, or large container support in a warm, humid, frost-free spot, since this hybrid is more cold-sensitive than many garden passionflowers and stops growing below about 60°F. Its most distinctive feature is foliage sprinkled with yellow nectar-gland spots and stripes on top and flushed purple beneath, setting it apart even before the small, bright orange, strongly camphor-scented flowers with green sepals open. Because it is of only moderate vigor compared to rampant species like P. caerulea, it suits a decorative trellis or large patio pot better than open ground where space is unlimited. Where winters dip near freezing, grow it in a container that can be moved under cover, or treat it as a conservatory and summer-patio plant.

common_name: Blueberry Glaze BerryBux (Compact Boxwood-Like Patio Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant from containers into acidic, well-drained potting mix or raised beds during dormancy or in early spring; Blueberry Glaze (marketed as BerryBux) is a compact Fall Creek Farm & Nursery Bushel and Berry selection bred to mimic a dwarf boxwood hedge while still bearing full-flavored fruit.

directions: Grow Blueberry Glaze in acidic, well-drained soil amended for azaleas and camellias, using its tight, fine-textured foliage as a low hedge, edging plant, or container specimen wherever a formal boxwood look is wanted alongside edible fruit. Small white spring flowers give way to berries that pass through yellow and red tones before ripening to a glossy dark blue, adding ornamental interest well before harvest. It needs a meaningful winter chill period to flower and fruit well, so it performs best in cooler climates than many other patio blueberries and is not a reliable choice where winters stay mild. Shear lightly after harvest to maintain its dense, rounded form, and keep the root zone consistently moist since the shallow, fibrous roots dry out quickly.
sources: Fall Creek Farm & Nursery — Bushel and Berry Collection Cultivar Information
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Blueberry Variety Profiles
Mississippi State University Extension — Blueberry Cultivars for the Home Garden
